title: Tokaj
description: Volcanic hills and river mists in north-east Hungary: the wine of kings, and the king of wines.
L: Volcanic hills where two rivers meet

Tokaj lies in north-east Hungary, near the Slovak and Ukrainian borders, in the foothills of the Zemplén mountains. The region covers about 27 villages and roughly 5,500 hectares of vines. A small part extends into Slovakia, which also uses the name Tokaj. The town of Tokaj sits where the Bodrog river meets the Tisza.

Tokaj has a continental climate: cold winters and warm summers, with long, dry, sunny autumns. The Bodrog and Tisza create autumn mists in the mornings, which burn off into warm afternoons. That combination is perfect for noble rot, Botrytis cinerea, which shrivels grapes and concentrates sugar and acidity.
What creates Tokaj's ideal conditions for noble rot?
River mists in the morning and sunny afternoons
The Bodrog and Tisza bring mist; the autumn sun dries the grapes.

Tokaj's hills are extinct volcanoes. Soils include rhyolite, andesite, tuff and clay, often covered with loess. Volcanic soils drain well and give mineral, smoky wines. Different hills have different soils, which is why Tokaj's vineyards were classified so early. Its cellars, cut into volcanic rock, are lined with a black mould.
Tokaj lies where the Bodrog meets the Tisza in north-east Hungary
River mists and sunny autumns favour noble rot
Volcanic soils give mineral, smoky wines

Furmint covers about 60 to 70% of Tokaj's vineyards. It has very high acidity, thin skins that become thinner as it ripens, and late ripening, all ideal for noble rot. It gives quince, apple, lemon, smoke and minerality when dry; honey, apricot and marmalade when sweet.

Hárslevelű, linden leaf, about 20 to 25%, adds perfume, honey and spice, with softer acidity. Sárgamuskotály, yellow Muscat, adds floral aromas in small amounts. Kövérszőlő, Zéta and Kabar are also allowed. Most Tokaji blends Furmint with Hárslevelű.
Match each grape to its role.
Hárslevelű's name means linden leaf. Its wines often smell of linden blossom and honey.
Furmint, about 60 to 70%, gives acidity and noble rot
Sárgamuskotály and others play minor roles
Explain how Tokaji Aszú is made

Aszú berries are grapes shrivelled by noble rot, picked one by one, often in several passes. They're collected and kept as a paste or whole. Then they're soaked in fermenting must or a base wine for 12 to 60 hours, extracting sugar and flavour. The mixture is pressed and fermented slowly, sometimes for months.
Botrytised berries soaked in base wine

Traditionally, sweetness was measured in puttonyos: the number of puttony, 25 kg hods of aszú berries, added to a 136-litre Gönci barrel of base wine, from 3 to 6. Since 2013, Tokaji Aszú must have at least 120 g/l of sugar, equal to the old 5 puttonyos; puttonyos labels of 5 and 6 are optional. Aszú ages at least 18 months in oak.
Put the making of Tokaji Aszú in order.
Pick botrytised berries one by one
Soak in base wine or must
Selection, soaking and slow fermentation give Aszú.

Tokaji Aszú is golden to amber, with apricot, orange marmalade, honey, saffron, ginger and tea. Sugar is balanced by Furmint's searing acidity, so it never feels cloying. It ages for decades, even a century or more.
What is the minimum sugar for Tokaji Aszú since 2013?
Aszú berries are soaked in base wine, then fermented slowly
Since 2013, Aszú needs at least 120 g/l of sugar

Szamorodni, a Polish word meaning as it comes, is made from whole bunches with some botrytised berries, not separated. It can be édes, sweet, or száraz, dry. Dry Szamorodni ages under a film of yeast, like Sherry's flor, in barrels not completely filled, giving nutty, oxidative notes. Sweet Szamorodni is lighter than Aszú.
As it comes: sweet or dry

Eszencia, or Esszencia, is the free-run juice that drips from aszú berries under their own weight, before soaking. It's extraordinarily sweet, often 450 to 800 g/l of sugar, and ferments for years, reaching only 3 to 5% alcohol. Tiny quantities are made. It's traditionally served by the spoon and was believed to have healing powers.
Match each wine to its making.
Tokaj makes several wines from one harvest.

Since the 2000s, Tokaj has made more dry wine, mainly from Furmint, from healthy grapes. It's mineral, smoky, with quince and citrus, and can be rich and textured, often compared with white Burgundy. Single-vineyard dry Furmint is now a major part of Tokaj's identity, especially as botrytis doesn't come every year.
Szamorodni uses whole bunches, sweet or dry
Eszencia is free-run juice, extraordinarily sweet
Dry Furmint is Tokaj's modern style

Tokaj's vineyards were classified from 1730, among the first in the world, into first, second and third class, based on soil, exposure and wine quality. In 1737, a royal decree defined the region's boundaries, making it one of the first closed, legally defined wine regions, before Portugal's Douro in 1756.

Top vineyards, dűlő, include Szarvas and Mézes Mály, once royal vineyards; Szent Tamás, Betsek and Úrágya. Labels increasingly name them, especially for dry Furmint and single-vineyard Aszú. The Hétszőlő and Disznókő estates are also famous names.
When was Tokaj's wine region legally defined by royal decree?

Tokaji Aszú was served at European royal courts; Louis XIV of France is said to have called it the wine of kings, the king of wines. After 1945, communist state farms took over, and quality fell. From 1990, private and foreign investors, like Royal Tokaji, Disznókő and Oremus, revived it. Tokaj became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002.
Tokaj's vineyards were classified before Bordeaux's 1855 classification.
Private estates revived it after 1990; UNESCO since 2002
Reading Tokaj and eating with it

Labels show Tokaji, the style, Aszú, Szamorodni, Eszencia or dry Furmint, sometimes puttonyos, 5 or 6, the vintage, the producer and often a vineyard, dűlő. Késői szüretelésű means late harvest, a lighter sweet style. Tokaji Aszú usually comes in a 50 cl bottle.

Tokaji Aszú suits foie gras, blue cheese, apricot tarts and fruit desserts; its acidity also works with spicy Asian food and Hungarian dishes with paprika. Dry Furmint suits fish, poultry, pork and goose. Dry Szamorodni suits nuts and aged cheese, like a Sherry. Serve sweet wines at 10 to 12 degrees.
Foie gras, blue cheese, apricot tart
Rich foie gras suits Aszú's sweetness and acidity.
An open bottle of Tokaji Aszú keeps for weeks in the fridge, thanks to its sugar and acidity.
Labels show the style, puttonyos and vineyard
Aszú suits foie gras and fruit desserts
Dry Furmint suits fish, poultry and pork
